title: The Opportunity Cost of Digging Deeper
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton uses an observed Do Now to argue that even good practice carries an opportunity cost. A teacher used mini-whiteboards, saw every student get Questions 1 to 3 right, yet spent eight minutes pressing students to explain their reasoning. That left too little time for Question 4, a table of values with negative numbers, where the whiteboards showed understanding was shaky, so the negative-value misconceptions were never addressed. Barton does not call the probing bad practice, since it gained information and signalled that reasoning matters, but asks whether it was the best use of those minutes. His rule is that when evidence shows understanding is secure on early questions and circulation suggests a later one is weak, the teacher should confirm and move on, saving time for where it is needed. If all questions prove secure, digging deeper is then fine.
points: Every teaching decision has an opportunity cost because time spent on one thing cannot be spent on another.
In the observed lesson, eight minutes of probing correct answers left no time to repair negative-number misconceptions on the one question students struggled with.
Pushing for excellence in explanations is valuable, but not when it displaces time from questions that most need teacher support.
Mini-whiteboards show where understanding is secure, and circulation shows where it may not be, together letting a teacher allocate finite time wisely.
Once understanding is confirmed across all questions, the teacher is free to dig deeper as before.
quotes: So, the teacher stuck with them, offering prompts and hints, but holding out for excellence.

Nothing the teacher did during those 8 minutes was bad practice or a waste of time. Indeed, pushing for excellence as he did, ensured he had extra information about the depth of his students’ understanding, and conveyed the message that in this classroom language and reasoning are important.
Every decision a teacher makes has an opportunity cost, as the time we spend doing one thing is time we cannot spend doing something else.
But, with one eye on the clock, and almost 20 minutes of the lesson gone, only felt he had time to do this for positive values of x.

The price he would pay for this is that he would not be able to probe the depths of his students’ understanding. But what he gains is 6 or 7 minutes that could be spent on the question that students most need his support on. I feel that would be a better use of our finite class time.
Then, if it turns out that understanding is secure for all questions, we are free to probe further in the exact way the teacher did.
